blindSummary:
Everyday legal exposure for trans visitors here is minimal. There are no traveller-facing restrictions: no bathroom law, no border issues, free movement within the regional visa-free area applies, and legal gender recognition has existed for over 40 years (though medicalised and historically requiring sterilisation). Police protect Pride events.

The climate is the concern. In October 2022, a radicalised teenager murdered two people outside an LGBT bar in the capital — classified as the country's first modern terrorist attack. The state responded seriously (terrorism charges, official condemnation), but anti-LGBT political rhetoric intensified afterwards rather than receding: the legislature advanced a bill to make legal gender recognition impossible (genetic-test-only basis), and constitutional amendments declaring gender immutable have been proposed. In July 2022 teenagers beat two men perceived as gay in the capital.

For a visitor: no legal exposure, functioning institutions, but elevated street-hostility risk and a political trajectory moving against trans recognition.
blindOutOfScope: The legal-gender-recognition ban bill and the constitutional gender amendments are resident-facing climate signals. Discrimination against a long-marginalised ethnic minority is out of scope.
blindLocalsOnly: The 40-year-old medicalised legal-gender-recognition regime and the ban bill are resident-facing.
blindSourceSummaries: NOTE: Not retrievable at research time (HTTP 401); the underlying newswire report (May 2023) covers this country's near-vote on banning legal recognition of transgender people.

Encyclopedia article on the 2022 capital shooting: a double murder outside an LGBT bar (12 October 2022); the perpetrator's manifesto was anti-LGBT; classified as a homophobic hate crime and as terrorism; domestic and international reactions.

Regional investigative-journalism network (Feb 2023): in the shadow of the attack, the situation of trans people in this country remains precarious - they were long subjected to harmful practices including forced sterilisation (required for document changes), and trans people remain a political target even after the terrorist attack on the LGBT bar.

International human-rights organisation (May 2023): the national legislature should reject a bill making legal gender recognition impossible - trans people have been able to access legal gender recognition here for more than 40 years, and the bill would remove this right in breach of international human-rights obligations.

Letter (April 2023) from the human-rights commissioner of a regional inter-governmental council to the national legislature: six months after the attack on the LGBT bar, no discernible progress; human rights of LGBTI people appear more, not less, at risk; concerned about regressive legislative proposals including the legal-gender-recognition ban bill.

National news outlet (May 2018): the largest survey to date of LGBT people's lives here - they 'often suffer from feelings of inferiority and depression because they are rejected by the public'; only half are willing to hold their partner's hand in public; a third identify with the dominant church.

National news outlet (June 2018): same-sex married couples have the right to stay in this country - the interior ministry responded to the top court of the supranational union this country belongs to, which held that a family member of a union citizen may reside with their spouse, including same-sex spouses married elsewhere.

Major polling organisation (Oct 2018): a multi-country survey of attitudes toward religion, minorities and key social issues across two broadly defined parts of a continent - fewer respondents in this country's part would extend marriage to gay or lesbian couples - comparative attitude data.
